- If sentiment turns negative or shows strong bearish signals (e.g., -1.00, 0.00, 0.67) in recent days, reduce forecasted price by 5–10% to account for downward momentum.  
- If model shows sharp upward spike (e.g., >75% above recent mean) followed by true outcome drop, apply “overshoot correction” — reduce forecast by 10–20% in next 5–7 days.  
- When sentiment is neutral or mixed (e.g., 0.00, 0.50, 0.67) and price is trending upward, expect mean reversion — cap forecast at 1–2 standard deviations above recent mean.  
- If true outcome consistently underperforms model (e.g., 3–5% below forecast for 3+ consecutive days), apply “lag correction” — reduce forecast by 2–5% for next 3–5 days.  
- In high volatility or event-driven periods (e.g., policy changes, market shocks), model tends to overreact — apply “event dampening” — reduce forecast by 5–15% if sentiment is neutral or mixed.  
- If sentiment is bullish (e.g., 1.00, 0.67) and model forecast is flat or declining, expect “sentiment-driven reversal” — increase forecast by 3–8% for next 3–5 days.  
- For long-term horizon (e.g., 30d) forecasts, if true outcome shows early mean reversion (e.g., 2–3 days below forecast), apply “early correction” — reduce forecast by 5–10% for next 5–7 days.
